title: A Hidden Limit of Space and Time Could Lead to Ultrafast Electronics
summary:
Quantum physics has a famous rule: you cannot know everything about a particle at once. Werner Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says that a particle's position and momentum cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. That limit is built into the laws of nature, not caused by faulty instruments.

But position and time are different. Heisenberg's rule does not restrict those two in the same way. Now researchers have shown experimentally that another limit exists: an electron's location and its behaviour over time cannot both be pinned down with unlimited precision. This new 'space-time limit' could matter a great deal for quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.

The discovery comes from an international team at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy in Germany, led by professors Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl and Klaus Richter, working with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.

To watch electrons move, the team built a new laser system that works like a high-speed camera. Timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface, just a few atomic diameters away. By changing the gap between two pulses, the researchers can see exactly when the electrons move. 'By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond,' said Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper.

The movements happen over attoseconds: one attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe. At these distances, electrons move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules.

What makes the result remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like tiny balls, they behave as quantum waves, letting them pass through an energy barrier even though classical physics says they should not have enough energy to cross it. This is quantum tunnelling, a bit like passing through a solid wall without breaking it. 'Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets,' said doctoral student and co-author Katharina Glöckl.
why_it_matters: Faster electronics could change computers and phones, and this experiment shows that the strange rules of quantum physics set the speed limits for the technology of the future.

background_read: Quantum physics is the science of the very smallest things, like electrons, which behave in ways that seem strange compared with everyday objects.
An electron is a tiny particle with a negative charge that moves around the centre of an atom.
A laser is a device that makes a narrow, powerful beam of light, and very short laser pulses can act like the flash of a super-fast camera.
Quantum tunnelling is when a particle passes through an energy barrier that it should not be able to cross, because it behaves like a wave rather than a tiny ball.
